blocks.prompt: The Joey the Size of a Jellybean
blocks.text: A baby kangaroo is born very small. It is about as big as a jellybean. It has no fur. Its eyes are still shut. The tiny joey crawls all the way up its mom's belly by itself. It finds her warm pouch and climbs in. It stays in there for months and grows. Fur grows in. Its eyes open. One day the joey pokes its head out and looks at the world. Later it hops out to nibble grass. When it gets scared, it dives back into the pouch, head first.

blocks.prompt: Built to Bounce
blocks.text: A kangaroo does not run. It hops, and it hops on two feet at once. That sounds like hard work. It is not. Inside a kangaroo's leg there are long, thick tendons that join muscle to bone. When the kangaroo lands, those tendons stretch like rubber bands. When it pushes off, they snap back and throw the kangaroo into the air. The tendons do a lot of the work, so the muscles do less. A big red kangaroo can cover twenty five feet in one hop. In a sprint it can reach forty miles an hour. At an easy pace it can bounce along for miles without getting tired. Its tail matters too. When a kangaroo slows down to graze, it leans back on its thick tail and swings both feet forward. Scientists watched kangaroos walk this way and measured the push. The tail pushes as hard as all four legs put together. It is not just a prop. It is a fifth leg.

blocks.prompt: Three Babies, Three Different Plans
blocks.text: A red kangaroo is born after about thirty three days. That is a shorter wait than most house cats manage. The newborn is roughly the size of a jellybean, pink, blind, and deaf, with no back legs worth mentioning. What it does have is two strong front arms. Using those arms alone, it hauls itself up through its mother's fur, unassisted, and finds the pouch. Inside, it latches onto a teat and does not let go for months. That is only the start of the strangeness. A mother kangaroo can carry three young at once, each at a different stage. One hops beside her and still comes back to nurse. One is fastened inside the pouch. And one is a tiny ball of cells, paused. Biologists call this pause embryonic diapause. The embryo simply stops developing and waits. If the season turns dry, or if the pouch is still occupied, it keeps waiting. When rain comes and the pouch empties, it starts growing again. Then comes the part that seems impossible. The joey outside needs rich, fatty milk to fuel all that hopping. The newborn inside needs thin, sugary milk. The mother makes both at the same time, from two different teats, in the same pouch. Each teat produces exactly what the young attached to it needs, and the recipe changes as that joey grows. None of this is sentimental. The red kangaroo lives in country where rain is a rumor for years at a time. A mother who can pause a pregnancy, restart it the week the grass greens, and feed two ages at once is a mother whose family survives the drought.

blocks.prompt: The Cheapest Way to Cross a Continent
blocks.text: Run faster and you burn more fuel. This is true for a horse, a dog, a mouse, and you. Every stride costs energy, and more strides per minute costs more energy per minute. Biologists took this rule as settled, because every animal they had ever put on a treadmill obeyed it. Then in 1973 two researchers, Terence Dawson and Richard Taylor, put a red kangaroo on a treadmill and turned up the speed. The kangaroo's oxygen use climbed at first, exactly as expected. Then, past about ten miles an hour, it stopped climbing. The kangaroo went faster and faster, and its energy cost flattened out and even dipped. It was getting more distance for the same fuel. The trick is in the ankle. A kangaroo's Achilles tendons are extraordinarily long and thick, and tendon is springy in the way a stretched rubber band is springy. When the animal lands, its whole body weight stretches those tendons, and the energy of the fall is not lost as heat, it is stored. On the next push off the tendons recoil and hand most of that energy back. Muscles still work, but they are topping up a spring rather than driving the animal from scratch. Faster hopping stretches the spring harder, and a harder stretched spring gives back more. A kangaroo at speed is closer to a bouncing ball than a running animal. There is a bonus. The impact of landing drives air out of the lungs and the recoil pulls it back in, so breathing comes along for the ride at almost no extra cost. Hopping and breathing lock into the same rhythm. Why would evolution bother? Look at where red kangaroos live. Inland Australia is enormous, flat, dry, and unreliable. Rain falls somewhere, but rarely where you are standing. An animal that must travel a hundred miles to the next green patch, and travel it on a nearly empty stomach, needs a way of moving that gets cheaper the more it is used. Hopping is that way. The kangaroo did not evolve a spring in order to be spectacular. It evolved a spring because the continent is wide and the grass is somewhere else.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Family Macropodidae, meaning big foot
Elastic tendon storage cuts the cost of speed
Dawson and Taylor, Nature, 1973
Procoptodon goliah stood over 6 feet tall
Hind legs are yoked: no walking backward
There are more kangaroos than people in Australia

blocks.prompt: A Continent's Answer to a Simple Problem
blocks.text: Every animal that moves has to answer the same question: how do I cross the distance between me and my next meal without spending more energy than the meal contains? Australia asked that question more harshly than most places. The interior is vast, flat, and dry, and its rainfall is not merely low but erratic. Grass appears somewhere, unpredictably, and an animal that cannot reach it dies. The kangaroo is one answer to that question, and it is an unusually elegant one. The answer is a spring. A kangaroo's Achilles tendons are long, thick, and stiff, and they behave like the tendons in nothing else its size. When the animal lands, its mass stretches them, and the energy of that landing is stored rather than wasted. The push off releases it. Muscle contributes, but much of the work is done by tissue that costs nothing to hold in tension. In 1973 Terence Dawson and Richard Taylor demonstrated the consequence on a treadmill: above a moderate speed, a red kangaroo's oxygen consumption stopped rising with speed. Going faster cost it nothing extra. No running mammal does this. The kangaroo's breathing is coupled to the same rhythm, the landing squeezing the lungs and the rebound refilling them, so even respiration is nearly free. Everything else about the animal follows from that spring. The tail, thick and muscular, is not decoration. When a kangaroo grazes it plants the tail and swings both feet through, and measurements show the tail supplies as much propulsive force as the four limbs combined. The hind legs are yoked together, which is why a kangaroo cannot walk backward on land, and why the emu and the kangaroo, both poor reversers, ended up on the national coat of arms in a story Australians enjoy telling. The pouch, the thirty three day pregnancy, the paused embryo, the two grades of milk from two teats at once: all of it is machinery for producing young cheaply and abandoning the effort instantly when the rain fails. But a spring has limits, and the fossils show where. Until about forty thousand years ago Australia carried Procoptodon goliah, a short faced kangaroo standing over six feet tall and weighing more than four hundred pounds. For decades it was drawn hopping. Then researchers examined its skeleton properly and found the ankle joints, the pelvis, and the tail all wrong for a hopper and right for something else: it probably walked, one enormous foot at a time. Tendons that store energy beautifully at ninety pounds tear at four hundred. The spring does not scale. Here is where the story stops being tidy. The red kangaroo is thriving. There are tens of millions of them, more kangaroos than Australians, because pastoralists dug watering holes across country that never had reliable water and removed the dingoes that hunted them. The animal on the coat of arms, the animal on the tail of the national airline, is also shot in the millions under government quota, and its meat and hide are sold. Australians argue about this constantly, and not stupidly. An ecologist points out that soft footed native grazers damage the soil far less than hard hooved cattle, and that a kangaroo harvest is arguably the most sustainable red meat on the continent. An animal welfare campaigner points out that a joey found in the pouch of a shot female is killed by hand, because there is nothing else to be done with it. Both are describing the same animal. The spring solved the continent. It did not solve us.
